thread.title: Separation Anxiety - Commentary Magazine

author: Tal Fortgang
title: Separation Anxiety - Commentary Magazine
text:
The late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia enjoyed tempering Americans’ obsession with the Bill of Rights. “It is a mistake to think that the Bill of Rights is the defining, or even the most important, feature of American democracy,” he argued at a 2008 symposium. He continued by recalling, as he regularly did, how many unfree countries have “parchment guarantees” of freedom, promises not worth the paper on which they were written. “Virtually all the countries of the world today have bills of rights. You would not feel your freedom secure in most of them.” Scalia wanted Americans to understand the “real” Constitution: “the provisions that establish the institutions of government” and whether they enable or prevent “the centralization of power in one man or one party.” The separation of power between legislative, executive, and judicial authorities is the true protection of liberty. Scalia would conclude with characteristic concision: “Structure is everything.”
Indeed, as constitutional theorists have argued for centuries—some would say millennia, pointing to Deuteronomy’s delegation of powers to king, priest, judge, and prophet—the separation of powers is logically prior to the realization of individual liberties. A powerful executive can run roughshod over your rights regardless of what the First Amendment says, unless some authority exists to push back. Even if you get your day in court, the proceedings will be shambolic if the judge answers to the prosecutor, or if the two of them report to the same boss.
Despite these principles obviously transcending partisanship, interest in the separation of powers in recent decades has primarily been the province of the legal and political right. Leading scholarship on separation came from professor-jurists like Scalia, who frequently found himself dissenting in cases softening the barriers between branches. The Federalist Society, which for half a century has served as the keystone of the conservative legal movement, lists “the separation of governmental powers” as its second of three guiding principles. Conservative critics fixated on the judiciary violating the separation of powers by “legislating from the bench.” The courts should enforce the separation of powers by wielding the non-delegation doctrine, such critics argued, which prevents the legislature from passing authorizations so broad that they effectively “delegate” legislative power to the executive.
While there are certainly many liberal and progressive scholars of constitutional structure, including some who take an orthodox view of separated powers (and its conceptual sibling, checks and balances), progressives often view the structural Constitution as an impediment to liberal progress. Some have inherited President Woodrow Wilson’s suspicion of a constitutional system with “its organs offset against each other, as checks,” while a long tradition of left-wing critics led by Richard Hofstadter and James Burns simply scorns outmoded constitutional design in favor of purer democracy. Progressives’ key policy achievements, moreover, were nearly all won through judicial fiat: same-sex marriage, abortion, increased protections for criminal defendants, even briefly the abolition of the death penalty. Increased delegations of legislative power to the ballooning administrative state were celebrated, especially when it came to regulating the environmental, financial, and health-care sectors.
Harvard professor Cass Sunstein is a liberal, not a progressive, but he has come to make a first-principles case for a robust conception of the separation of powers. He deserves one cheer for trying to talk a Democratic Party ensorcelled by dreams of constitutional overhaul off the ledge in his aptly titled new book, Separation of Powers. It’s not obvious that he would. Sunstein is a technocrat by training. He was President Obama’s Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs coordinator—a distinctly unglamorous title for a hugely important position—determining which rules made by unelected experts would attain the force of law. He described any number of unrealized social advances he thought government could encourage in the best-known of his manifold previous books, Nudge. Yet while he thinks that conservatives and Republicans have misapplied the concept of separated powers in marginal cases, most of his book naturally militates against the progressive left’s dismissal of structural separationism as outdated, obstructionist, and even anti-democratic.
_____________
Even two cheers, however, would be excessive, since Sunstein’s account of the separation of powers loses its vigor when it encounters areas of potential pushback from the left-liberal mainstream—and contains oversights so glaring that Sunstein’s analysis verges on misleading.
Sunstein’s main contribution is pointing out that there is no one “separation of powers,” but six separations, each with its own liberty-preserving functions. Each barrier represents the exercises of power that are off-limits to branches other than the one to whom the power is assigned. For example, there are two separations of power that limit the executive branch: It may not exercise the legislative power (vested in Congress) or the judicial power (province of the courts).
Of course, as Sunstein recognizes and discusses, the executive branch does both. The administrative state (a maligned “fourth branch”) writes detailed regulations that look a lot like legislation, making trade-offs between important policy considerations and carrying the full force of law. You can hold a physical copy of the Code of Federal Regulations—or at least you could if you were a powerlifter. The CFR is approximately 190,000 pages, full of rules whose violation will result in prison or fines. If the federal government determines that you violated one or more of those rules, it may bring legal action against you in an administrative law court, where judges who work for the agency, not the judiciary, will determine your fate. Sunstein seems a bit perturbed by these apparent violations of one-third of the separations of power but is less interested in calling for them to be remedied than in understanding the justifications for those separations—even as they are increasingly consigned to the realm of the hypothetical.
Those justifications tend to revolve around preserving liberty, which Sunstein defines as “allow[ing] people to be something like sovereigns over their own lives.” The Constitution and its framers made the same connection. “There can be no liberty where the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person,” wrote James Madison. Sunstein adds important color, especially with his focus on “deliberative democracy.” To get Congress to pass a law, the president to enforce it, and the judiciary to uphold it, no one can simply force his or her will upon the people. Rather, “institutions are designed to increase the likelihood that decisions would be based…on the force of the better argument.” You have to justify making new rules in language that will be intelligible and compelling to all branches. One could add, with the underappreciated political theorist Martin Diamond, that our Constitution requires broad consensus among different factions, different social and economic classes, and different kinds of government officials. Building a consensus through public reason minimizes the chances that government will trample individual rights, or simply govern stupidly or rashly.
This is where things get surprising, even a bit maddening. Given Sunstein’s multifaceted appreciation for the separation of powers, one might naturally assume that he is a strict separationist who stands zealously on guard for breaches of the constitutional system. Not so. Justice Scalia, the godfather of contemporary originalism, nonetheless described himself as a “fainthearted originalist.” One could diagnose Sunstein’s approach to the separation of powers in similar terms.
For one thing, Sunstein barely mentions the problem of judges “legislating from the bench,” a phenomenon so pronounced over the last century that it alone may have revived popular interest in constitutional structure. Cabining the judicial role should play a central role in a political philosophy that revolves around “deliberative democracy.” Sunstein is keen to point out that federal judges lack the information, accountability, and authorization to make major public policy decisions, but he makes no effort to describe an approach to judging that would follow from his premises.
If he had, it would probably look a lot like textualism, the interpretive theory that tethers judges to the law ratified by elected representatives. Sunstein is adamantly not a textualist. He therefore licenses judges to take some steps toward writing laws for themselves—probably the most egregious violation of the separation of powers, subordinating the first branch, the locus of federal lawmaking, to the third branch and its unelected jurists.
For another thing, Sunstein takes a rhetorically strong stand against the legal theory that builds the strongest wall of separation between the legislative and executive branches. The nondelegation doctrine, which holds that Congress may not grant the president “essential legislative functions,” has not factored into a Supreme Court decision since 1935—but threatens to rid executive agencies of their power to write wide-ranging and detailed regulations that look a lot like legislative acts. Sunstein calls this bright-line defense of legislative primacy “a terrible, awful, stinky idea.” Strong words. Indeed, Sunstein criticizes the “Grand Narrative” of an imperial executive emerging through legislative abdication, agency independence, and administrative adjudication.
But his critique is altogether very gentle. He ends up admitting that the Grand Narrative leads people to vigilance about separation of powers, which is a good thing, all else being equal. So why won’t Sunstein join them? He thinks there is a long tradition of its violation and that reversing it would be “arrogant and wrong.” He adds that his brand of “pragmatist” believes “Congress ought to be given some room to adopt institutional arrangements, consistent with the broad commitment to separation of powers, that are, in its view, necessary or appropriate.” This begs the question, though. Are the facts alleged by the Grand Narrative, if true, consistent with the separation of powers?
For someone who has written a whole book about the importance of separationism, Sunstein goes remarkably soft in defending the division of power. He doesn’t muster much more vigor fending off the charge that the modern administrative state violates a long tradition that predated the last fourscore years of executive branch growth. Sunstein claims the mantle of pragmatism, which seems warranted: Pragmatists are less concerned with systems than they are with outcomes; Sunstein cares about whether things have worked, and will continue to work, reasonably well. That is his prerogative, but it does make an odd conclusion for a book about constitutional structure.
One additional omission casts a shadow on Separation of Powers: Where are the states? Political scientists refer to our federalist system, which reserves most political power for the states, as vertical separation of powers. States do most of the governing in our constitutional order, and their interactions with federal law and policy are complex, interesting, and dynamic. Yet Sunstein’s book contains no analysis on how the principles of separationism shape the extent of state plenary powers, federal preemption, or a host of other issues in our separate-sovereign system.
This omission reveals the failure of Sunstein’s approach. Sunstein attempts to show how the six separations work together as a system, to achieve James Madison’s first two goals of government. “You must first enable the government to control the governed,” the great constitutional framer wrote in Federalist No. 51, “and in the next place oblige it to control itself.” Government does not exist merely to provide liberty through deliberative democracy, though those are important. It must provide order, protection, and justice while still upholding its liberal-democratic commitments. States take the lead in that system by regulating social and economic behavior, and providing courts of general jurisdiction, while allowing Americans to vote with their feet by moving to the states that appeal to them most. Each branch and each level of government represents a crucial cog in this complex machine. To overlook one completely is necessarily to give an incomplete—indeed a misleading—view of what each component of government must, may, or cannot do.
Ultimately, Sunstein’s book fails to provide what lay readers interested in constitutional structure need, which is an account of what each of the powers looks like: How can we know the difference between essentially legislative, executive, and judicial powers based on their key characteristics? How can we assess whether an action is best undertaken by a state or the federal government, and where can we draw bright lines between permissible executive action and impermissible encroachment on Congress’s turf? If we had a clear view of how the system as a whole is meant to operate—taking seriously the role of states and the strictly delineated assignments of each federal branch—we could try to deduce the principles that tell us whether government is acting consistently with, or in violation of, our sacrosanct constitutional principles. And we could avoid relying on logical fallacies and misdirections to defend violations we find politically desirable.
Until we can do that, the most crucial questions about which political arrangements are constitutionally acceptable will go unanswered, and the separation of powers will serve as little more than a parchment guarantee against those disinclined to feel bound by it.
